package greetings

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    <ins>"math/rand"</ins>
)

// Hello returns a greeting for the named person.
func Hello(name string) (string, error) {
    // If no name was given, return an error with a message.
    if name == "" {
        return name, errors.New("empty name")
    }
    // Create a message using a random format.
    message := fmt.Sprintf(<ins>randomFormat()</ins>, name)
    return message, nil
}

<ins>//

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "log"

    "example.com/greetings"
)

func main() {
    // Set properties of the predefined Logger, including
    // the log entry prefix and a flag to disable printing
    // the time, source file, and line number.
    log.SetPrefix("greetings: ")
    log.SetFlags(0)

    // Request a greeting message.
    message, err := greetings.Hello("Gladys")
    // If an error was returned, print it to the console and
    // exit the program.
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }

    // If no error was returned, print the returned message
    // to the console.
    fmt.Println(message)
}

$ go run .
Great to see you, Gladys!

$ go run .
Hi, Gladys. Welcome!

$ go run .
Hail, Gladys! Well met!

internal_slots.source: Managing connections

For the vast majority of programs, you needn't adjust the ⟦P0⟧ connection⟦P1⟧pool defaults. But for some advanced programs, you might need to tune the⟦P2⟧connection pool parameters or work with connections explicitly. This topic⟦P3⟧explains how.

The ⟦P0⟧⟦P1⟧⟦P2⟧ database handle is safe for⟦P3⟧concurrent use by multiple goroutines⟦P4⟧(meaning the handle is what other languages might call “thread-safe”). Some⟦P5⟧other database access libraries are based on connections that can only be used⟦P6⟧for one operation at a time. To bridge that gap, each ⟦P7⟧ manages a pool⟦P8⟧of active connections to the underlying database, creating new ones as needed⟦P9⟧for parallelism in your Go program.

The connection pool is suitable for most data access needs. When you call an⟦P0⟧⟦P1⟧ ⟦P2⟧ or ⟦P3⟧ method, the ⟦P4⟧ implementation retrieves an⟦P5⟧available connection from the pool or, if needed, creates one. The package⟦P6⟧returns the connection to the pool when it's no longer needed. This supports a⟦P7⟧high level of parallelism for database access.
Setting connection pool properties ⟦P0⟧
You can set properties that guide how the ⟦P0⟧ package manages a connection⟦P1⟧pool. To get statistics about the effects of these properties, use⟦P2⟧⟦P3⟧⟦P4⟧⟦P5⟧.
Setting the maximum number of open connections ⟦P0⟧

⟦P0⟧⟦P1⟧⟦P2⟧⟦P3⟧imposes a limit on the number of open connections. Past this limit, new⟦P4⟧database operations will wait for an existing operation to finish, at which⟦P5⟧time ⟦P6⟧ will create another connection. By default, ⟦P7⟧ creates a⟦P8⟧new connection any time all the existing connections are in use when a⟦P9⟧connection is needed.
Keep in mind that setting a limit makes database usage similar to acquiring a⟦P0⟧lock or semaphore, with the result that your application can deadlock waiting⟦P1⟧for a new database connection.
Setting the maximum number of idle connections ⟦P0⟧
⟦P0⟧⟦P1⟧⟦P2⟧⟦P3⟧changes the limit on the maximum number of idle connections ⟦P4⟧⟦P5⟧maintains.

When an ⟦P0⟧ operation finishes on a given database connection, it is not⟦P1⟧typically shut down immediately: the application may need one again soon, and⟦P2⟧keeping the open connection around avoids having to reconnect to the database⟦P3⟧for the next operation. By default an ⟦P4⟧ keeps two idle connections at⟦P5⟧any given moment. Raising the limit can avoid frequent reconnects in programs⟦P6⟧with significant parallelism.
Setting the maximum amount a time a connection can be idle ⟦P0⟧
⟦P0⟧⟦P1⟧⟦P2⟧⟦P3⟧sets the maximum length of time a connection can be idle before it is closed.⟦P4⟧This causes the ⟦P5⟧ to close connections that have been idle for longer⟦P6⟧than the given duration.

By default, when an idle connection is added to the connection pool, it⟦P0⟧remains there until it is needed again. When using ⟦P1⟧ to⟦P2⟧increase the number of allowed idle connections during bursts of parallel⟦P3⟧activity, also using ⟦P4⟧ can arrange to release those⟦P5⟧connections later when the system is quiet.
Setting the maximum lifetime of connections ⟦P0⟧
Using ⟦P0⟧⟦P1⟧⟦P2⟧⟦P3⟧sets the maximum length of time a connection can be held open before it is⟦P4⟧closed.

By default, a connection can be used and reused for an arbitrarily long amount⟦P0⟧of time, subject to the limits described above. In some systems, such as those⟦P1⟧using a load-balanced database server, it can be helpful to ensure that the⟦P2⟧application never uses a particular connection for too long without reconnecting.
Using dedicated connections ⟦P0⟧
The ⟦P0⟧ package includes functions you can use when a database may⟦P1⟧assign implicit meaning to a sequence of operations executed on a particular⟦P2⟧connection.

The most common example is transactions, which typically start with a ⟦P0⟧⟦P1⟧command, end with a ⟦P2⟧ or ⟦P3⟧ command, and include all the⟦P4⟧commands issued on the connection between those commands in the overall⟦P5⟧transaction. For this use case, use the ⟦P6⟧ package’s transaction support.⟦P7⟧See ⟦P8⟧Executing transactions⟦P9⟧.

For other use cases where a sequence of individual operations must all execute⟦P0⟧on the same connection, the ⟦P1⟧ package provides dedicated connections.⟦P2⟧⟦P3⟧⟦P4⟧⟦P5⟧ obtains a dedicated⟦P6⟧connection, an ⟦P7⟧⟦P8⟧⟦P9⟧. The⟦P10⟧⟦P11⟧ has methods ⟦P12⟧, ⟦P13⟧, ⟦P14⟧,⟦P15⟧⟦P16⟧, ⟦P17⟧, and ⟦P18⟧ that behave like the⟦P19⟧equivalent methods on ⟦P20⟧ but only use the dedicated connection. When finished⟦P21⟧with the dedicated connection, your code must release it using ⟦P22⟧.

internal_slots.source: Opening a database handle

The ⟦P0⟧⟦P1⟧⟦P2⟧ package simplifies⟦P3⟧database access by reducing the need⟦P4⟧for you to manage connections. Unlike many data access APIs, with⟦P5⟧⟦P6⟧ you don't explicitly open a connection, do work, then close⟦P7⟧the connection. Instead, your code opens a database handle that represents⟦P8⟧a connection pool, then executes data access operations with the handle,⟦P9⟧calling a ⟦P10⟧ method only when needed to free resources, such as those⟦P11⟧held by retrieved rows or a prepared statement.

In other words, it's the database handle, represented by an⟦P0⟧⟦P1⟧⟦P2⟧⟦P3⟧, that⟦P4⟧handles connections, opening and closing them on your code's behalf. As your⟦P5⟧code uses the handle to execute database operations, those operations have⟦P6⟧concurrent access to the database. For more, see⟦P7⟧⟦P8⟧Managing connections⟦P9⟧.
⟦P0⟧Note:⟦P1⟧ You can also reserve a database connection. For more⟦P2⟧information, see⟦P3⟧⟦P4⟧Using dedicated connections⟦P5⟧.
In addition to the APIs available in the ⟦P0⟧ package, the Go⟦P1⟧community has developed drivers for all of the most common (and many uncommon)⟦P2⟧database management systems (DBMSes).
When opening a database handle, you follow these high-level steps:
Locate a driver.
A driver translates requests and responses between your Go code and the⟦P0⟧database. For more, see ⟦P1⟧Locating and importing a database driver⟦P2⟧.
Open a database handle.
After you've imported the driver, you can open a handle for a specific⟦P0⟧database. For more, see ⟦P1⟧Opening a database handle⟦P2⟧.

Overview ⟦P0⟧
This document includes decisions the Go Security team has made about⟦P0⟧various commonly-reported issues. It mostly serves as a reference⟦P1⟧for things we do not consider to be a vulnerability.
This list is not comprehensive.
General principles ⟦P0⟧
Not every bug is a vulnerability.
For any bug, it is almost always possible to construct⟦P0⟧a hypothetical scenario in which it causes a vulnerability.

For example, imagine a bug in an image decoder which causes it to⟦P0⟧incorrectly decode some inputs. Now imagine a hypothetical system⟦P1⟧which accepts pictures of written cheques and makes bank transfers⟦P2⟧to satisfy the cheques. If this system contains a gateway which validates⟦P3⟧the request and a backend which performs the transfer, a parser⟦P4⟧differential in the image decoders used by the gateway and backend⟦P5⟧could result in the gateway passing a malicious operation on to the⟦P6⟧backend.

Classifying an image misparsing bug as a vulnerability based on this⟦P0⟧scenario does not serve any useful purpose. Warning users that they⟦P1⟧are affected by a "vulnerability" of this nature is just noise,⟦P2⟧since few to no users will actually be affected. Calling this a⟦P3⟧vulnerability is detrimental to security, since it trains users to⟦P4⟧ignore reports as mostly meaningless.

This scenario is also an example of why we do not assign severity⟦P0⟧labels to security issues: To the hypothetical cheques processor⟦P1⟧this may be a high-severity issue, but to most users it is not an⟦P2⟧issue at all.
As a general principle, simply being able to construct a⟦P0⟧hypothetical scenario in which a bug causes a security issue⟦P1⟧is not sufficient cause for us to handle it as a security issue itself.
Vulnerabilities ⟦P0⟧
Remote Code Execution ⟦P0⟧
A scenario which permits an attacker to execute code in a situation⟦P0⟧where code execution is not expected is a PRIVATE-track vulnerability.⟦P1⟧This supersedes all other decisions.
This decision does not cover functions which are expected to execute code.
Covered:
A parse function which executes code on a malicious input.
A malicious request causing the ⟦P0⟧ server to execute code.
Not covered:
The ⟦P0⟧ command runs tests. Running ⟦P1⟧ on attacker-controlled⟦P2⟧tests is not within our threat model.
Panics ⟦P0⟧
A panic when processing attacker-controlled input may be a vulnerability.
A panic in a server expected to handle attacker-controlled requests,⟦P0⟧such as a ⟦P1⟧ server, is usually a PRIVATE-track vulnerability.
A panic in a client, such as a ⟦P0⟧ client, is usually a PUBLIC-track⟦P1⟧vulnerability.
A panic in a parse function in a package which handles plausibly⟦P0⟧malicious input, such as ⟦P1⟧ or ⟦P2⟧,⟦P3⟧is usually a PUBLIC-track vulnerablity.
An input which causes a panic due to its natural size,⟦P0⟧such as a very large image, is usually not classified as a vulnerability.

internal_slots.source: ⟦P0⟧ 140-3 Compliance

Starting with Go ⟦P0⟧, Go binaries can natively operate in a mode that⟦P1⟧facilitates ⟦P2⟧ 140-3 compliance. Moreover, the toolchain can build against⟦P3⟧frozen versions of the cryptography packages that constitute the Go⟦P4⟧Cryptographic Module.

⟦P0⟧ ⟦P1⟧ 140-3 is a ⟦P2⟧. Government compliance regime for cryptography⟦P3⟧applications that amongst other things requires the use of a set of approved⟦P4⟧algorithms, and the use of⟦P5⟧⟦P6⟧⟦P7⟧⟦P8⟧-validated⟦P9⟧cryptographic modules tested in the target operating environments.

⟦P0⟧⟦P1⟧:⟦P2⟧ Simply using a ⟦P3⟧ 140-3 compliant and validated cryptographic module⟦P4⟧may not—on its own—satisfy all relevant regulatory requirements. The Go Cryptographic Module is a collection of standard library Go packages⟦P0⟧under ⟦P1⟧ that implement ⟦P2⟧ 140-3 approved⟦P3⟧algorithms.

When operating in ⟦P0⟧ 140-3 mode:

The Go Cryptographic Module automatically performs an integrity self-check at⟦P0⟧⟦P1⟧ time, comparing the checksum of the module's object file computed at⟦P2⟧build time with the symbols loaded in memory.
All algorithms perform known-answer self-tests according to the relevant ⟦P0⟧⟦P1⟧140-3 Implementation Guidance, either at ⟦P2⟧ time, or on first use.

⟦P0⟧⟦P1⟧⟦P2⟧ is implemented in terms of a⟦P3⟧⟦P4⟧ ⟦P5⟧ ⟦P6⟧ ⟦P7⟧. To guarantee the same level of security as programs not⟦P8⟧running in ⟦P9⟧ 140-3 mode, random bytes are also sourced from the platform's⟦P10⟧⟦P11⟧ at every ⟦P12⟧ and mixed into the output as uncredited additional⟦P13⟧data.

⟦P0⟧⟦P1⟧⟦P2⟧ with⟦P3⟧⟦P4⟧⟦P5⟧⟦P6⟧ will cap the length⟦P7⟧of the salt at the length of the hash.

internal_slots.source: Go Fuzzing technical details
This document provides an overview of the technical details of the native fuzzing implementation, and is intended to be a resource for contributors.
General architecture

The fuzzer uses a single coordinator process, which manages the corpus, and multiple worker processes, which mutate inputs and execute the fuzz target. The coordinator and worker processes communicate using a piped JSON-based ⟦P0⟧ protocol, and shared regions of virtual memory.

For each worker the coordinator creates a goroutine which spawns the worker process and sets up the cross-process communication. Each goroutine then reads from a shared channel which is fed by the main coordinator loop, sending instructions it reads from the channel to the relevant worker processes.

The main coordinator loop picks inputs from the corpus, sending them to the shared worker channel. Whichever worker picks up that input from the channel will send a fuzzing request to the corresponding worker process. This process sits in a loop, mutating the input and executing the fuzz target until an execution either causes an increase in the coverage counters, causes a panic or crash, or passes a predetermined deadline.

If the worker process executes a mutated input which causes an increase in coverage counters or a recoverable panic, it signals this to the coordinator which is then able to reconstruct the mutated input. The coordinator will attempt to ⟦P0⟧minimize the input⟦P1⟧, then either add it to the corpus for further fuzzing, in the case of finding increased coverage, or write it to the testdata directory, in the case of an input which causes an error or panic.

If a non-recoverable error occurs while fuzzing which causes the worker process to shut down (⟦P0⟧. infinite loop, ⟦P1⟧, memory exhaustion, etc), minimization will not be attempted, and the failing input will be written to the testdata directory and reported.
Sequence diagram of the interaction between coordinator and worker, as described above.
Cross-process communication

When spawning the child worker processes, the coordinator sets up two methods of communication: a pipe, which is used to pass JSON-based ⟦P0⟧ messages, and a shared memory region, which is used to pass inputs and ⟦P1⟧ state. Each worker process has its own pipe and shared memory region.

The ⟦P0⟧ pipe is used by the coordinator to control the worker process, sending it either fuzzing or minimization instructions, and by the worker to relay results of its operations to the coordinator (⟦P1⟧. whether the input expanded coverage, caused a crash, was successfully minimized, etc).

The shared memory region is used to pass specific information back and forth with the workers. The coordinator uses the region to pass the corpus entry to fuzz to the worker, and is used by the worker to store its current ⟦P0⟧ state. The ⟦P1⟧ state is used by the coordinator to reconstruct the mutations that were applied to the input by the worker when it has finished executing the target (this reconstruction happens both when the worker exits cleanly, and when it crashes.)
Input selection
The coordinator currently does not implement any advanced form of input prioritization. It cycles through the entire corpus, looping after it exhausts the entries.
Similarly, the coordinator does not implement any type of corpus minimization (not to be confused with input minimization, ⟦P0⟧discussed below⟦P1⟧).
Coverage guidance

The fuzzer uses ⟦P0⟧⟦P1⟧ compatible⟦P2⟧ inline 8 bit coverage counters. These counters are inserted during compilation at each code edge, and are incremented on entry. Counters are not protected against overflow, so that they don't become saturated.

Similarly to ⟦P0⟧ and ⟦P1⟧, when tracking coverage, the counters are quantized to the nearest power of two. This allows the fuzzer to differentiate between insignificant and significant changes in execution flow. In order to track these changes, the fuzzer holds a slice of bytes which map to the inline counters, the bits of which indicate if there is at least one input in the corpus which increments the related counter at least 2^bit-position times. These bytes can become saturated, if there are inputs which cause counters to hit each quantized value, at which point the related counter fails to provide further useful coverage information.

As coverage counters are added to every edge during compilation, code not being fuzzed is also instrumented, which can cause the worker to detect coverage expansion that is unrelated to the target being executed (for instance if some new code path is triggered in a goroutine unrelated to the fuzz target). The worker attempts to reduce this in two ways: firstly it resets all counters immediately before executing the fuzz target and then snapshots the counters immediately after the target returns, and secondly by explicitly ignoring a set of packages which are likely to be "noisy"
A number of packages explicitly do not have counters inserted, since they are likely to introduce counter noise that is unrelated to the target being executed. These packages are:
Mutation engine

When the worker receives a new input, it applies mutations to the input before executing the target with the input. After each mutation, the fuzz target is executed with the new input, and if coverage is not expanded, further mutations are applied. In order to prevent inputs from massively diverging from their initial state, after five mutations are applied to an input, it is reset to its original state before further mutations are applied. For example for the input ⟦P0⟧, the mutation strategy may look like the following:
The mutators attempt to bias towards producing smaller inputs, rather than larger inputs, in order to prevent rapid growth of the corpus size.
There are numerous mutators for ⟦P0⟧ and ⟦P1⟧ types, and a smaller number of mutators for all the ⟦P2⟧, ⟦P3⟧, and ⟦P4⟧ types.
There are currently no execution driven mutation strategies implemented (such as input-to-comparison correspondence), nor dictionary based mutators.
Input minimization

In order to prevent the corpus from ballooning (which bogs down the fuzzer both in terms of performance, and reducing the probability that a mutation will actually touch interesting data) we attempt to minimize each input discovered which expands coverage or causes a recoverable crash (non-recoverable crashes, such as those caused by memory exhaustion, are not minimized, as the process would be extremely slow). The employed strategy for minimization is rather simple, sequentially attempting to remove bytes from the input while maintaining the initial coverage found. In particular the minimization mechanism uses the following strategy:
Attempt to cut an exponentially smaller chunk of bytes off the end of the input
Attempt to remove each individual byte
Attempt to remove each possible subset of bytes
Attempt to replace each non-human readable byte with a human readable byte (⟦P0⟧. something in the ⟦P1⟧ set of bytes)

The coordinator will attempt to ⟦P8⟧minimize the input⟦P9⟧, then either add it to the corpus for further fuzzing, in the case of finding increased coverage, or write it to the testdata directory, in the case of an input which causes an error or panic.⟦P10⟧If a non-recoverable error occurs while fuzzing which causes the worker process to shut down (⟦P11⟧. infinite loop, ⟦P12⟧, memory exhaustion, etc), minimization will not be attempted, and the failing input will be written to the testdata directory and reported.⟦P13⟧Sequence diagram of the interaction between coordinator and worker, as described above.⟦P14⟧Cross-process communication⟦P15⟧When spawning the child worker processes, the coordinator sets up two methods of communication: a pipe, which is used to pass JSON-based ⟦P16⟧ messages, and a shared memory region, which is used to pass inputs and ⟦P17⟧ state. Each worker process has its own pipe and shared memory region.⟦P18⟧The ⟦P19⟧ pipe is used by the coordinator to control the worker process, sending it either fuzzing or minimization instructions, and by the worker to relay results of its operations to the coordinator (⟦P20⟧. whether the input expanded coverage, caused a crash, was successfully minimized, etc).⟦P21⟧The shared memory region is used to pass specific information back and forth with the workers. The coordinator uses the region to pass the corpus entry to fuzz to the worker, and is used by the worker to store its current ⟦P22⟧ state. The ⟦P23⟧ state is used by the coordinator to reconstruct the mutations that were applied to the input by the worker when it has finished executing the target (this reconstruction happens both when the worker exits cleanly, and when it crashes.)⟦P24⟧Input selection⟦P25⟧The coordinator currently does not implement any advanced form of input prioritization. It cycles through the entire corpus, looping after it exhausts the entries.⟦P26⟧Similarly, the coordinator does not implement any type of corpus minimization (not to be confused with input minimization, ⟦P27⟧discussed below⟦P28⟧).⟦P29⟧Coverage guidance⟦P30⟧The fuzzer uses ⟦P31⟧⟦P32⟧ compatible⟦P33⟧ inline 8 bit coverage counters. These counters are inserted during compilation at each code edge, and are incremented on entry. Counters are not protected against overflow, so that they don't become saturated.⟦P34⟧Similarly to ⟦P35⟧ and ⟦P36⟧, when tracking coverage, the counters are quantized to the nearest power of two. This allows the fuzzer to differentiate between insignificant and significant changes in execution flow. In order to track these changes, the fuzzer holds a slice of bytes which map to the inline counters, the bits of which indicate if there is at least one input in the corpus which increments the related counter at least 2^bit-position times. These bytes can become saturated, if there are inputs which cause counters to hit each quantized value, at which point the related counter fails to provide further useful coverage information.⟦P37⟧As coverage counters are added to every edge during compilation, code not being fuzzed is also instrumented, which can cause the worker to detect coverage expansion that is unrelated to the target being executed (for instance if some new code path is triggered in a goroutine unrelated to the fuzz target). The worker attempts to reduce this in two ways: firstly it resets all counters immediately before executing the fuzz target and then snapshots the counters immediately after the target returns, and secondly by explicitly ignoring a set of packages which are likely to be "noisy"⟦P38⟧A number of packages explicitly do not have counters inserted, since they are likely to introduce counter noise that is unrelated to the target being executed. These packages are:⟦P39⟧Mutation engine⟦P40⟧When the worker receives a new input, it applies mutations to the input before executing the target with the input. After each mutation, the fuzz target is executed with the new input, and if coverage is not expanded, further mutations are applied. In order to prevent inputs from massively diverging from their initial state, after five mutations are applied to an input, it is reset to its original state before further mutations are applied. For example for the input ⟦P41⟧, the mutation strategy may look like the following:⟦P42⟧The mutators attempt to bias towards producing smaller inputs, rather than larger inputs, in order to prevent rapid growth of the corpus size.⟦P43⟧There are numerous mutators for ⟦P44⟧ and ⟦P45⟧ types, and a smaller number of mutators for all the ⟦P46⟧, ⟦P47⟧, and ⟦P48⟧ types.⟦P49⟧There are currently no execution driven mutation strategies implemented (such as input-to-comparison correspondence), nor dictionary based mutators.⟦P50⟧Input minimization⟦P51⟧In order to prevent the corpus from ballooning (which bogs down the fuzzer both in terms of performance, and reducing the probability that a mutation will actually touch interesting data) we attempt to minimize each input discovered which expands coverage or causes a recoverable crash (non-recoverable crashes, such as those caused by memory exhaustion, are not minimized, as the process would be extremely slow). The employed strategy for minimization is rather simple, sequentially attempting to remove bytes from the input while maintaining the initial coverage found. In particular the minimization mechanism uses the following strategy:⟦P52⟧Attempt to cut an exponentially smaller chunk of bytes off the end of the input⟦P53⟧Attempt to remove each individual byte⟦P54⟧Attempt to remove each possible subset of bytes⟦P55⟧Attempt to replace each non-human readable byte with a human readable byte (⟦P56⟧. something in the ⟦P57⟧ set of bytes)⟦P58⟧

Please do not send LLM-generated reports without proper curation.

Modern LLMs are very good at finding real and important security bugs.⟦P0⟧Unfortunately, they are also very good at finding imaginary issues, or real⟦P1⟧issues that are ⟦P2⟧not security bugs⟦P3⟧. ⟦P4⟧⟦P5⟧output is often verbose, buries important information in irrelevant text, and⟦P6⟧contains grandiose and unsupportable claims.

Sending us dozens of⟦P0⟧possible security issues while relying on us to find the one significant result⟦P1⟧hidden among them asks us to do the curation, and ultimately hinders our goal of⟦P2⟧making Go secure. Editors integrated with the ⟦P0⟧Go language server⟦P1⟧, such as ⟦P2⟧⟦P3⟧ Code with the Go extension⟦P4⟧, can detect vulnerabilities in your dependencies.
There are two modes for detecting vulnerabilities in dependencies. Both are backed by the ⟦P0⟧Go vulnerability database⟦P1⟧ and complement each other.

Imports-based analysis: in this mode, editors report vulnerabilities by scanning the set of packages imported in the workspace, and surface the findings as diagnostics in the ⟦P0⟧ files. This is fast, but may report false positives in case your code imports the packages that contain vulnerable symbols but the functions with the vulnerability are not reachable. This mode can be enabled by the ⟦P1⟧⟦P2⟧⟦P3⟧ gopls setting.

⟦P0⟧ analysis: this is based on the ⟦P1⟧⟦P2⟧⟦P3⟧ command-line tool, which is embedded in ⟦P4⟧.  This provides a low-noise, reliable way to confirm whether your code actually invokes vulnerable functions. Because this analysis can be expensive to compute, it must be manually triggered by using the "Run govulncheck to verify" code action associated with the diagnostic reports from the Import-based analysis, or using the ⟦P5⟧⟦P6⟧⟦P7⟧ code lens on ⟦P8⟧ files.

Notes and Caveats

The extension does not scan private packages nor send any information on private modules. All the analysis is done by pulling a list of known vulnerable modules from the Go vulnerability database and then computing the intersection locally.
The import-based analysis uses the list of packages in the workspace modules, which may be different from what you see from ⟦P0⟧ files if ⟦P1⟧ or module ⟦P2⟧⟦P3⟧⟦P4⟧ is used.
